newsitem.title: JAPAN: DIC insurance may cover bank debentures -- Japan MOF.
newsitem.headline: DIC insurance may cover bank debentures -- Japan MOF.

text.p: Bank debentures issued by long-term credit banks may be covered by Japan's Deposit Insurance Act which was revised last year, Finance Ministry (MOF) officials said on Thursday.

Under the Deposit Insurance Act, which is aimed at protecting depositors, bank debentures are not included in calculating the insurance premiums paid by financial institutions and holders of the debentures are not protected.

However, rules in the revised act make it possible for the Finance Minister to protect holders of bank debentures until March 31, 2001 using insurance premiums if a financial institution issuing bank debentures merges due to financial difficulties, the officials said.
A MOF officials said there were no instances in sight requiring insurance coverage for debentures.
"As for the bank which has been recently rumoured in the financial markets to have financial problems, the ministry will firmly support its efforts to restructure," he said.
While he did not identify the bank, Nippon Credit Bank, one of the three long-term credit banks in Japan, is known to be facing a heavy burden of problem loans.

Whether creditors holding bank debentures are protected or not has become a heated issue since Taku Yamasaki, a senior official of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, said recently that creditors holding bank debentures may be protected through the use of various types of government funds.
An official at a major commercial bank said it would not be fair if creditors holding bank debentures were protected by the deposit insurance system.

"It is not fair that a major bank pays some 15 billion yen in insurance premiums a year. But the premiums paid by a long-term credit bank are only one-tenth of that amount since bank debentures are not counted in calculating insurance premiums," he said.
Long-term credit banks raise funds through selling debt to investors rather than taking in deposits.
